clue.text: CV giving complete references

wordplay.note: C is the abbreviation for chapter and V for verse, so the two letters stand for the two words, joined by 'and'

explanation.surface: A job applicant's CV comes with a full set of references attached.
explanation.walkthrough: CV looks like a curriculum vitae, but read as two abbreviations it is C and V, chapter and verse.
explanation.definitionFit: To give chapter and verse is to cite a source exactly and in full, as with a Bible citation.

clue.text: Cleverly, say, incriminate best shot

indicators.note: something shot is wrecked or broken, so the letters before it fall apart and are rebuilt

parts.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone acting cleverly might gather the evidence that best incriminates a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleverly' is not an adverb but James Cleverly, a British Conservative politician who held senior government posts; 'say' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: James Cleverly served as Foreign Secretary and Home Secretary, so he is an example of a senior government member.

clue.text: Men fitting plug reordered electrical component

indicators.note: reordered tells the solver to take the three pieces in a different sequence from the one the clue gives them

parts.note: a plug is a piece of publicity, an advert, shortened to AD
fitting means suitable
OR is other ranks, the ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Workmen fit a plug and then rearrange a part of the electrical system.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives men, fitting, plug; reordering them back to front puts plug first.
explanation.definitionFit: An adaptor is a device that lets a plug fit a different socket, so it is a component of electrical equipment.

clue.text: Shaking a coin tin close to bus conductor

indicators.note: shaking jumbles the contents, so these letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is wanted

parts.note: the last letter of bus

explanation.surface: Someone rattles a collecting tin near a bus conductor, hoping for a coin.
explanation.walkthrough: The conductor is not on a bus but in front of an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: Arturo Toscanini was a famous Italian orchestral conductor, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Decide to do this a second time

definitions.meaning: first meaning: make up one's mind

definitions.text: to do this a second time
definitions.meaning: second meaning: read as RE plus SOLVE, to work out this clue again

explanation.walkthrough: 'This' refers to the clue itself: solving it again is re-solving it.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means to settle on a course of action, and split with a hyphen it means to work out again.

clue.text: Heard about any trouble involving India's eternal foe

indicators.note: something heard about is known by sound, so the phrase that follows is spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: trouble is a mess, and India is I in the NATO alphabet, so India's is I'S; involving simply joins them

explanation.surface: We hear of trouble concerning India and its long-standing enemy.
explanation.definitionFit: A nemesis is an arch-enemy who keeps returning to defeat someone, a lasting adversary.

clue.text: Price of kitbag is completely eclipsed by uniform

indicators.note: something completely eclipsed is blotted out and its place taken, so one part gives way to another

parts.note: a valise is a travelling bag
taken as written, the letters to be taken out
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Asking the price of a kitbag that is entirely overshadowed by a uniform in a military shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Value is what something is worth, the amount it would fetch, so it is a synonym for price.

clue.text: Sells disheartened rescue dogs

indicators.note: removing a word's heart strips out its whole inside, leaving just the outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of rescue
to dog someone is to follow them closely, to tail them

explanation.surface: Animal shelter dogs left downhearted, waiting for adoption.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rescue dogs' reads as one noun phrase, but rescue is fodder and dogs is a verb meaning follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A product that retails at a price sells to the public in shops for that amount.

clue.text: Note softened her up — reaching breaking point

definitions.note: the phrase is usually 'at the end of one's tether'

indicators.note: up here means in disorder or amiss, so the preceding letters are scrambled

parts.note: the fifteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A kind note calmed down a woman who was close to snapping.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes having no patience or endurance left, which is the state of being about to snap.

clue.text: Audacity of Spurs' wingers going after two cups

indicators.note: going after means following, so this piece is placed behind the other one

parts.note: a bra has two cups

indicators.note: wingers play out on the flanks, so only the letters on the edges of the word count

parts.note: the first and last letters of Spurs

explanation.surface: Tottenham Hotspurs' wide players boldly chasing a cup double.
explanation.walkthrough: Spurs is the nickname of Tottenham Hotspur, a London football club; the cups are underwear, not trophies.
explanation.definitionFit: Brass is informal British for cheek or nerve, as in 'brass neck', so it means boldness.

clue.text: Mock short Disney film's boring plot — Dumbo's debut

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the film's title goes inside the other piece

parts.note: a plot of land is a site

indicators.note: short means cut off before its end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: Mulan is a Disney animated film

indicators.note: a debut is a first appearance, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of Dumbo

explanation.surface: A scornful critic says the short Disney film's plot is dull and only Dumbo's first appearance livens it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' and 'plot' read as criticism of a story, but plot is a piece of land and boring means drilling in.
explanation.definitionFit: Mock as an adjective means imitation or fake, as in a mock exam, which is what simulated means.

clue.text: Clear everyone is following introduction to board game

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this piece is placed behind the one it follows

parts.note: to clear a sum as profit is to net it

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the first letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of board
everyone is all

explanation.surface: Clearing the table so everyone can follow the rules of a new board game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board game' looks like one phrase, but board only supplies a letter and game alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Netball is a team sport, popular in Britain and the Commonwealth, where players shoot a ball into a raised ring.

clue.text: Lawman is going back over the woman's fines

indicators.note: over here means covering, so one piece is placed around the next
going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read from end to start

parts.note: taken as written
the possessive pronoun for a woman
F is an abbreviation for fine, so doubling it makes the plural

explanation.surface: A lawman going back to review the fines a woman has incurred.
explanation.walkthrough: F for fine is the pencil-grade abbreviation; doubling a letter abbreviation makes a plural, as pp for pages.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheriff is a law-enforcement officer, especially in the American West, so he is a lawman.

clue.text: End it with European six-footer

parts.note: a term is a limit or end
taken as written
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A plea to finish things off with a very tall European.
explanation.walkthrough: A six-footer sounds like a tall person, but here it is a creature with six feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Termites are insects, and every insect has six legs, which makes it a creature with six feet.

clue.text: Relative intervenes when one becomes old

indicators.note: becomes says one thing turns into another, so a letter is swapped for a different one

parts.note: to intervene is to step in, here in the third person
the Roman numeral for one
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A family member steps in once someone grows old.
explanation.definitionFit: A stepson is the son of one's spouse from an earlier relationship, a relation by marriage.

clue.text: From that day on Church follows English translation with nothing missing

indicators.note: follows means comes after, so this piece is placed at the end

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English

indicators.note: missing means absent, so that letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: a translation is a version of a text
O looks like zero, nothing
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Since one day the Church has followed an English translation of scripture complete and unabridged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With nothing missing' reads as complete, but it means the O is removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever since means continuously from a particular time until now, the same as from then on.

clue.text: It's my round — getting shot of whisky, finally inspiring …

indicators.note: getting shot of something means getting rid of it, so that letter is removed

parts.note: a pub round is the drinks you pay for, so the speaker says they are buying

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the last letter of whisky

explanation.surface: A pub-goer announces their round, a shot of whisky, and it leads into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot of whisky' looks like a drink, but 'getting shot of' means discarding. The ellipsis links the clue to 19 across in the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbue is to fill or permeate with a feeling or quality, as to inspire someone with courage.

clue.text: Slow cycling through swamp for one of obstinate courage

indicators.note: through means passing inside, so one piece sits within the other
cycling means going round, so the first letter moves to the end of the word

parts.note: dull means sluggish or slow
a bog is a swamp

explanation.surface: Cycling slowly through a swamp takes stubborn determination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' looks like riding a bike, but it moves the first letter of the word to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulldog is used of a tenacious, stubborn person, as in the British bulldog spirit associated with Churchill.

clue.text: Perhaps dial 999 and put empty gesture on the record

indicators.note: put together with on is an instruction to place one piece in position relative to the rest
in a down answer on means placed above, so this piece comes first
an empty word has its contents removed, leaving only its outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of gesture
taken as written
LP is a long-playing record

explanation.surface: Someone calls the emergency number and makes a hollow gesture for the record.
explanation.walkthrough: 999 is the UK emergency telephone number, like 911 in the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling the emergency services is one way to summon assistance, so the definition is an example of the phrase.

clue.text: … sad songs recalling date army charged on shed

indicators.note: charged means loaded or filled, so one piece is packed inside the other
recalling means calling back, so the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: to date someone is to see them

indicators.note: shed means cast off, so those letters are dropped from the word

parts.note: a legion is an army
taken as written, the letters to be dropped

explanation.surface: Mournful songs remembering the day an army stormed a hut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' looks like a building, but it is a verb telling you to cast off a word's ending. The leading ellipsis continues 16 across in the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: An elegy is a mournful poem or song of lament, often for the dead.

clue.text: Saloon maybe seen on drive after erratic motorist initially gets ban

indicators.note: in a down answer on means placed above, so this piece sits over the next
after means following, so these pieces come behind the first
initially means at the start, so only the first letters of the words before it are taken

parts.note: the first letters of erratic and motorist
a saloon is one kind of bar
drive means energy or push, go

explanation.surface: A reckless driver spotted in a saloon car on the road ends up banned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saloon' suggests a car next to motorist and drive, but it is a bar; a saloon is the British name for a sedan.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official prohibition, especially on trade, so it is a kind of ban.

clue.text: Press stories left out examples of subtle humour

parts.note: to press clothes is to iron them

indicators.note: out means removed or excluded, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: stories in the sense of untruths
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Newspaper stories omitted the gentle jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press stories' reads as newspaper reports, but press is a verb for smoothing clothes and stories are fibs.
explanation.definitionFit: Irony is humour in which words mean the opposite of what they seem, so ironies are instances of that wry wit.

clue.text: Not so foul proposition — not so wrong

indicators.note: not here rejects one word in favour of another, so that pair of letters is swapped for a replacement

parts.note: to proposition someone is to solicit them
taken as written, the letters to be replaced
foul in the sense of bad, ill

explanation.surface: An indecent suggestion that is less offensive is also less sinful.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part as 'not so, (but) foul': in the word for proposition, SO gives way to ILL. The repeated 'not so' just softens the definition in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Illicit means forbidden by law or morality, hence improper or wrong.

clue.text: Turned up to support shy South American native

indicators.note: in a down answer a supporting piece goes underneath, so it comes second

parts.note: coy means bashful

indicators.note: turned means flipped round, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone turned up to back a bashful South American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' looks like arrived; split, turned flips the word up.
explanation.definitionFit: The coypu is a large aquatic rodent native to South America, also called nutria.

clue.text: On reflection it's part of the Kop's ebullient custom

indicators.note: a reflection shows things the other way round, so the letters run backwards
part of says the answer is a piece taken from inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run of letters spanning Kop's and the start of ebullient

explanation.surface: Thinking it over, being excitable is part of the Kop's tradition.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kop is the famous home terrace at Liverpool's Anfield football ground; the definition is custom as in custom-made.
explanation.definitionFit: Bespoke means made to a particular customer's order, like a custom-built item or tailored suit.

clue.text: Dry debate about toy

indicators.note: about suggests moving around, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: the nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A dull argument about a plaything.
explanation.definitionFit: A teddy bear is a soft stuffed bear, a classic child's plaything.

clue.text: Sound like a hack's nearly swallowing pill

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: nigh means near or almost
E is slang for an ecstasy tablet

explanation.surface: A sound like a journalist nearly choking on a tablet.
explanation.walkthrough: A hack sounds like a journalist, but here it is a hired horse.
explanation.definitionFit: A hack is an ordinary riding horse, and the noise a horse makes is a whinny.

clue.text: One whose chair was set up by the throne

definitions.text: One whose chair was set up by the throne

parts.words: One whose chair was set up by the throne
parts.note: surface reading: someone whose seat was placed next to a monarch's throne; setter's reading: an academic chair, a professorship, founded by the Crown

explanation.walkthrough: 'Chair' and 'throne' suggest furniture side by side; in fact the chair is a university post and 'by' means created by royal authority.
explanation.definitionFit: In British universities, chiefly Oxford, Cambridge and Scottish ones, certain professorships were founded or are appointed by the monarch, and their holders bear a Latin title meaning royal.
